questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the matrix $Q$ given below?

- $Q$ is **not** a singular matrix
- $Q$ is a singular matrix
- $det(Q)=-5$

$$
Q=[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 & 6 \\ 1 & 4 & 7 \\ 2 & 5 & 8\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that a square matrix is singular if its determinant is equal to $0.$

Using the formula, we take the alternating sum of the entries in the top row of the matrix, multiplied by their respective minors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(Q) & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 & 6 \\ 1 & 4 & 7 \\ 2 & 5 & 8\end{aligned}| \\  & =0|\begin{aligned}4 & 7 \\ 5 & 8\end{aligned}|-3|\begin{aligned}1 & 7 \\ 2 & 8\end{aligned}|+6|\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}| \\  & =0-3(8-14)+6(5-8) \\  & =0-3\cdot (-6)+6\cdot (-3) \\  & =18-18 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(Q)=0$, the matrix is singular. 

Therefore, only statement II is true.

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the matrix $T$ given below?

- $T$ is a singular matrix
- $det(T)=-3$
- $T$ is **not** a singular matrix

 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ -2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that a square matrix is singular if its determinant is equal to $0.$

Using the formula, we take the alternating sum of the entries in the top row of the matrix, multiplied by their respective minors, as follows:  

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ -2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =4|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}|-2|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}|-1|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =4(2+3)-2(1+6)-1(-1+4) \\  & =4\cdot 5-2\cdot 7-1\cdot 3 \\  & =20-14-3 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $det(T)=3\ne 0$, the matrix is **not** singular. 

Therefore, only statement III is true.

$$
\begin{aligned}det & =|\begin{aligned}x & 2x-1 & 6 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ -1 & x+1 & -4\end{aligned}| \\  & =x|\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ x+1 & -4\end{aligned}|-(2x-1)|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -1 & -4\end{aligned}|+6|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ -1 & x+1\end{aligned}| \\  & =x(3\cdot (-4)-0\cdot (x+1))-(2x-1)(0)+6(0\cdot (x+1)-3\cdot (-1)) \\  & =x(-12)+0+6(3) \\  & =-12x+18\end{aligned}
$$

Since the matrix is singular, the determinant is $0,$ and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-12x+18 & =0 \\ -12x & =-18 \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Given that the determinant of $[\begin{aligned}x & 2x & 5 \\ 3 & x & 4 \\ 7 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]$ is $40$, find all the possible values of $x$ **in ascending order**.

In ascending order, $x=$
{{field-1}} and $x=$
{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let’s use our formula to find an expression for the determinant in terms of $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}x & 2x & 5 \\ 3 & x & 4 \\ 7 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =x|\begin{aligned}x & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|-2x|\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 7 & 2\end{aligned}|+5|\begin{aligned}3 & x \\ 7 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =x(2x-4)-2x(3\cdot 2-4\cdot 7)+5(3-7x) \\  & =x(2x-4)-2x(-22)+15-35x \\  & =2{x}^{2}-4x+44x+15-35x \\  & =2{x}^{2}+5x+15\end{aligned}
$$

Since the determinant of the matrix is $40$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+5x+15 & =40 \\ 2{x}^{2}+5x-25 & =0 \\ x & =\frac{-5\pm \sqrt{{5}^{2}-4(2)(-25)}}{2(2)} \\ x & =\frac{-5+\sqrt{225}}{4} \\  & =\frac{-5\pm 15}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, **in ascending order**, the solutions are $x=-5$ and $x=\frac{5}{2}.$
